01 — What RackTrack does

One photo of a rack.
Everything that is in it.

Point your phone at a rack and take a single photo. RackTrack works out what is inside — every slot, every device, every port — and checks it against your records.

Finding one port in a datacenter is slow, awkward work. You stand in a cold aisle with a torch, counting slots from the top rail, squinting at a label, hoping the spreadsheet is right. Get it wrong and you unplug something that matters.

RackTrack replaces the counting. It reads the photo the way an experienced engineer reads a rack, then points at the exact port you asked for.

Start here

02 — How it works

Photo in. Rack map out.

You never see any of this. It matters only because it explains what the app can and cannot know — which is worth understanding before you trust it.

What happens to your photo

Everything in the middle comes from your photo alone. That is why scanning works in a basement with no signal, on a brand-new account, with nothing configured.

The two boxes on the right are different. They are RackTrack checking its answer against something outside the photo — your records, and the switch itself. Those are the parts that need setting up, and the parts that can fail on their own.

The whole journey, end to end

From no account to a written-up ticket
Why the distinction matters

If the Ports screen says it cannot reach the switch, your scan is still perfectly good. One is a photo; the other is a network connection. They fail separately — and this guide tells you which is which on every page.

03 — Getting in

Two ways to get an account.

Either you bring your company onto RackTrack, or somebody invites you to one that is already there.

PATH A

Create a company

You are the first one here. Fill in your email, a username, your company's name and a password. RackTrack emails you a six-digit code. You become the administrator.

PATH B

Accept an invitation

Someone sent you a link. Your email is already filled in and locked. Choose a username and a password, and you are in — straight to the scan screen.

Three things that catch people out

The six-digit code lasts one minute — have your inbox open before you ask for it. An invitation link works once and dies after seven days. And a brand-new company must be approved before anyone in it can scan — nobody is emailed about that, so go and tell whoever runs RackTrack that you are waiting.

The first time you open the app

A short tour runs on first open — four slides, about fifteen seconds. It covers exactly the three things this guide covers next.

1 · Scan a rack Point the camera at the rack, or upload a photo, and press Scan.
2 · Review the results See each device, where it sits in the rack, and its details.
3 · Check the ports Open Ports to see the switch live — what is free, what is connected.

Skip dismisses it, and it does not come back.

04 — Taking the photo

The photo decides
how good the answer is.

So the app does not let you take a bad one. It watches the picture while you aim, and names the single thing to fix.

The quality gate — why the shutter sometimes will not fire
The most common “the app is broken”

If pressing the shutter seems to do nothing at all, the app is not broken — one of the three checks has not passed. Read the line of text under the box. It is telling you exactly what to fix.

Which mode do I want?

Choosing between Single, Multi and Video

Four rules of thumb

Stand square to the rack, not off to one side — a side-on photo hides the ports. Hold level with the middle of the rack, not up high or down low. Get the whole rack in, top rail to bottom rail. And if cables hang over the front, take extra photos from the left and the right so the app can see behind the bundles.

Rescanning costs nothing

Photograph the same rack twice and RackTrack recognises it, handing back the earlier result instantly — with any corrections you made still applied.

05 — Reading the result

Finding one port
in a rack of forty.

This is the job the app was built for. You have been handed a port number, and you need to put your finger on that exact port.

How you find the port

STEP 1

Pick the device

From the list, or just tap its box in the photo.

STEP 2

Pick the port type

RJ45, SFP, Console or USB. Only the types that device actually has are offered.

STEP 3

Type the number

The app zooms your photo to that exact port, and dims everything else.

What it tells you about that port

ReadingWhich means
Status Connected — there is a cable in it. Empty — there is not.
Cable and Color What kind of cable, and what colour it is. Genuinely useful when following a run by eye.
Linked endpoint What is on the far end. Marked LIVE, because the app asked the switch — it did not read this from the photo.
It checks its own work

The app asks “Port 23 on Switch. Right?”, with a Yes and a No. Saying No fixes your result on the spot — and teaches the model, so it gets better at your equipment over time. Ten seconds well spent.

06 — Six ways to see a rack

The same rack,
six different questions.

Once a rack is scanned it can be opened six ways. Three read your photo. Three talk to the live network.

From the photo — works anywhere, no setup

Photo

Overview

What is in this rack — and where exactly is the port I need?

Photo

Topology

How it is laid out, and what is cabled to what. In 2D and 3D.

Photo

Switches

Make, model, datasheet — and whether the firmware is current.

From the live network — needs setup

Live

Ports

What is plugged in right now, and which ports are genuinely free.

Live

Network

What the network itself says is alive in this rack.

Live

Drift

What has changed since last time — and exactly when.

The one people end up relying on

Drift answers “but it worked yesterday”. When a cable is quietly re-patched to a different machine overnight, it is on the record — even if nobody owns up to it.

One honest limit

A patch panel has no electronics in it, so the switch cannot see it — and neither can RackTrack. A cable looks like it runs straight from the switch to the far end. That is physics, not a missing feature.

07

07 — Working from a ticket

It already knows which port
the ticket is about.

Connect ServiceNow and your open incidents appear on the scan screen. Link a scan to one, and the app stops making you hunt.

The ticket loop, end to end

What changes when a ticket is linked

Before the scan RackTrack reads the labels in your photo and confirms you are at the rack the ticket names. Wrong rack, and it stops you — showing what it read beside what it expected.
After the scan No device list, no counting. It lands straight on the port the incident is about.
While you work The port is polled every five seconds. The moment the cable goes live, the app says so — with the time it happened.
Afterwards It drafts the work note, shows you a preview, and posts it to the incident.
The point of all this

A technician arrives holding a ticket. Today that means finding the rack, finding the switch, counting to port 23, doing the work, then writing it up later from memory. With RackTrack the ticket is the workflow — and the write-up is done before they leave the aisle.

Read the note before you send it

The work note lands on a real ticket that other people read and act on. RackTrack shows you a preview first, and tells you how confident it is. It is confident, not infallible.

08 — Your team

Company, sites, people.

RackTrack is organised the way your business already is. A scan belongs to the site of whoever took it.

How an organization is put together

Who can do what

RoleWhat they can do
Member
most people		 Scan racks and read the results. Sees their own scans.
Site managerThe same as a member.
Organization admin All of the above — plus add sites, invite people, connect ServiceNow or your records database, use the Marketplace, and see every scan in the company.
Platform owner Everything, across every company. Approves new companies as they sign up.
Tell your admins this

RackTrack does not email invitations for you. The admin copies the link and sends it themselves. If nobody sends the link, nobody joins — it is the most common reason a rollout stalls.

09 — What needs setting up

What works on day one.
And what needs an admin.

Where every screen gets its information

The setup, in full

To unlockSomebody has to
Ports and Drift Save the switch's sign-in details once. RackTrack uses a read-only account — it can look, but it cannot change anything on your switch. Drift works with TP-Link today.
Network Run a Netdisco discovery server on your network.
Tickets and records Connect ServiceNow — or NetBox, SolarWinds, Spectrum, or your own database.

Connecting a system

An admin opens Connections, presses + Add connection, picks the type and fills in the credentials. There is no test button — saving is the test; watch the message that follows it.

One at a time

Only one connection is active at a time, and every screen reads from it. Switching it switches the source of all your data — RackTrack does not blend two systems together.

30 days
you stay signed in
1 min
sign-up codes expire
7 days
invite links expire

10 — When something goes wrong

Find your symptom.

Nearly every question RackTrack gets asked is one of these.

Getting in

What you seeWhyWhat to do
Stuck on Waiting for approvalYour company is not approved yet. Go and tell whoever runs RackTrack. They are not emailed about it.
The word rate_limitedToo many tries in one minute.Wait 60 seconds.
The six-digit code will not workIt expired — codes last one minute. Ask for a new one and use it straight away.
Your invitation link failsUsed already, or over seven days old. Ask for a fresh one. The old one cannot be revived.

Scanning

What you seeWhyWhat to do
The shutter does nothingOne of the three quality checks has not passed. Read the hint under the box and fix the one thing it names.
No shutter button at allYou are on an iPad or a computer. Use Upload, or take the photo on a phone.
Devices missing from the resultShot at an angle, or cables are hiding them. Retake square-on; add photos from the left and right.
Progress sits at 88%Nothing is wrong — the bar is an estimate, not a measurement. Wait.

The live screens

What you seeWhyWhat to do
“The switch didn't respond”You are not on the same network as the switch. Get off the guest wifi and onto the right network.
“Lost the SSH session”Most switches allow only one connection at a time. Retry in a moment.
Network view never loadsNo discovery server has been set up. Ask an admin. It will never load until one exists.
Drift says “Waiting for first poll…” for everNo switch is being watched. Ask an admin to set one up.
A free-looking port says Reserved It has a name written on it, so somebody has claimed it. Check with the switch's owner before you take it.
